The fight had happened on Sunday in their house in Nashik's old town, over Devika's plan to go to a friend's birthday in the city.

By Wednesday, Devika was telling her cousin, "Papa said I could never go anywhere. Never. He shouted it."

That same evening, Tushar was telling his wife, "I only said not this Sunday. I never said never. And I didn't shout."

At dinner the argument started again. "You said never!" "I said this Sunday!" Both were red in the face, both completely sure.

Devika's grandmother put down her roti. "I was in the next room. I heard 'not this time' and I heard both of you get loud. That's all I know for sure."

Devika and Tushar looked at each other, suddenly less certain.

qa.q: Where did Devika want to go?
qa.a: To a friend's birthday in the city.

qa.q: Why was Devika so sure her father said "never"?
qa.a: She felt hurt and angry after the fight, and those feelings shaped her memory so it seemed like he had said never.

qa.q: What could Devika and Tushar try the next time they remember an argument differently?
qa.a: Each could say "this is how I remember it" and talk about the real issue, instead of fighting over the exact words.

qa.q: How might Devika's grandmother see the argument?
qa.a: She seems calm and fair, and tries to show that each of them remembers it through their own feelings.

grounding: A teenager and parent each remember an argument differently and both feel certain, as feelings reshape memory.

On the bus home in Gothenburg, Ingrid replayed the argument from breakfast. Her father Pablo had said, "You're always on that phone and never help." She was sure. The words stung all day.

That evening, she brought it up. "You said I never help."

Pablo frowned. "I said, 'Could you help more with dishes?' That's it."

"No. You said never."

"Ingrid, I remember. I was tired, but I didn't say never."

They stared at each other. Ingrid felt her throat tighten. She had been angry all day about words he says he didn't say. Pablo rubbed his forehead. "Maybe I sounded harsher than I meant. And maybe you heard it bigger than I said it."

In the school counsellor's room, Eshaan sat on one chair and his father Yogesh on the other. They had been sent there after shouting at each other in the car park.

"He said I'm a disappointment," Eshaan said, arms folded.

"I said I was disappointed in the marks," Yogesh said. "Not in you."

"You said me."

"I didn't!"

The counsellor waited. "Both of you were very upset. Upset people often remember the words that hurt most, and sometimes remember them stronger than they were said."

Eshaan looked at the floor. Yogesh sighed. "Whatever I said, I don't think you're a disappointment. I was scared about the exams."

Eshaan's shoulders dropped a little.

Last month my college friends and I were arguing about our first-year trip to Goa. I was absolutely sure Rukmini had worn a yellow dress on the last night, when we sang on the beach. I could see it clearly, the colour, the frill on the sleeve.

"No, it was blue," Rukmini said.

"It was yellow. I'm certain."

I'm Sarita. These days, when I'm certain, I try to remember the blue dress.

I'm Manjula, and people ask me how my sister Dilnaz and I stopped fighting about our childhood. We used to argue for hours. She'd say Ammi punished her more. I'd say it was me. Each of us had our story and we were both sure.

Last month she told a story about my wedding I don't remember at all. I just listened. It's her memory. She doesn't have to prove it.

Francis, you're asking why I'm careful when I ask children questions at the school? Let your Karthik uncle tell you about when I was eight.

A window in our lane got broken. The neighbour came to me and said, "You saw the Sharma boy throw the stone, didn't you? A big stone?" I hadn't seen anything. But she asked again, "A big stone, yes?" I nodded, because she was an adult and she seemed sure.

The next day the Sharma boy was punished. Later we found out a ball had hit the window during cricket.

I felt sick. Now, when I talk to children, I only ask, "What did you see?" Then I listen.

You asked what to do about the argument over what happened at Nani's funeral. Here's what I've learnt.

When everyone is upset, memories get tangled. I don't ask, "Didn't Mama say this?" because that pushes people to agree. I ask, "What do you remember?" and I listen.

After Nani's funeral I wrote down what happened that same evening, the times and who said what. It helped later when people remembered it differently.

And when Masi said she felt blamed, I didn't argue about the exact words. The hurt was real. I told her so.

Try asking open questions. Write things down early. And be kind about feelings, even when details don't match.

Indu

My name's Jomon, and I help run a small community mediation group. Last month two neighbours, Ira and her building's secretary, came in angry about a fight over parking.

Ira was sure the secretary had shouted "Get out!" He was sure he'd only said, "Please move." Both were shaking.

I didn't ask, "Did he shout at you?" That puts words in her mouth. I asked each, "What happened, from the start?" and wrote it down right there.

Ira's voice cracked when she described feeling humiliated. I told her the feeling mattered, even if we couldn't be sure of each word.

The notes showed they'd both misunderstood the parking rule. Once they saw that, they could stop fighting about the shouting.

qa.q: What were Ira and the secretary angry about?
qa.a: A fight over parking.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when her voice cracked?
qa.a: Ira was feeling humiliated and hurt by the argument.

qa.q: Why did Jomon ask "What happened, from the start?" instead of "Did he shout at you?"
qa.a: An open question lets each person tell their own version without being pushed toward a detail.

qa.q: How might the secretary have felt when Jomon listened to both sides equally?
qa.a: He probably felt calmer and treated fairly, which helped him drop the argument about shouting.

grounding: A wise mediator avoids leading questions, records accounts right away and treats strong feelings as real without taking every detail as proof.
